fact_text: You usually have to pay Council Tax on the home you live in if you are aged 18 or over.
evidence_quote: You’ll usually have to pay Council Tax if you’re 18 or over.

fact_text: If you are the only adult liable in your home (for example, if you live on your own) you get 25% off your Council Tax bill, but you must apply to your local council for it as it is not applied automatically.
evidence_quote: You’ll get 25% off your bill if you pay Council Tax and either:

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: Council Tax is a fixed charge per property. Actually: a household with only one liable adult gets 25% off, and 'disregarded' people (such as full-time students) are not counted towards the adult total. Action required: apply to your local council — the discount is not applied automatically.

fact_text: A household where everyone is a full-time student does not have to pay Council Tax and can apply for an exemption if it receives a bill.
evidence_quote: Households where everyone’s a full-time student do not have to pay Council Tax.

fact_text: State schooling in England is free: every child aged between 5 and 16 is entitled to a free place at a state school.
evidence_quote: All children in England between the ages of 5 and 16 are entitled to a free place at a state school.

fact_text: You apply for a state school place through the local council for the area where you will live — including when applying from another country — not to the school directly.
evidence_quote: If you’re applying from another country, contact the local council in the area where you’re going to live.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you apply to the school you want your child to attend. Actually: state school applications go through the local council for the area you will live in, even when applying from abroad. Action required: contact that local council to apply, not the school.

fact_text: Children who arrive after the school year has started are admitted through an 'in-year application' made to the local council, which can advise which schools still have places.
evidence_quote: Contact your local council to find out about applying for a school place once the school year has started (known as in-year applications).

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: a family arriving mid-year must wait for the next admissions round or apply to schools directly. Actually: they apply to the local council as an 'in-year application' at any time. Action required: ask the local council which schools have places and how to apply.

fact_text: For the normal admissions round, applications for a primary school place open in September and must be submitted by 15 January of the following year.
evidence_quote: Applications open in September each year and close on 15 January.

fact_text: If your driving licence is from a country that is not 'designated', you may drive in Great Britain for 12 months from becoming resident; after that you must apply for a GB provisional licence and pass the theory and practical driving tests.
evidence_quote: After 12 months, you’ll need to apply for a GB provisional licence and pass the theory driving test and practical driving test to drive in Great Britain.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you can keep driving indefinitely on your home-country licence. Actually: with a licence from a non-designated country you may drive in Great Britain for only 12 months from becoming resident, then must pass the GB theory and practical tests. Action required: plan to sit the GB driving tests within the first year.

fact_text: Only licences from the listed 'designated countries or territories' can be exchanged for a GB licence without retaking a test; the current list is Andorra, Australia, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Canada, Cayman Islands, Falkland Islands, Faroe Islands, Gibraltar, Hong Kong, Japan, Monaco, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Republic of Moldova, Republic of North Macedonia, Singapore, South Africa, Switzerland, Taiwan, Ukraine, United Arab Emirates and Zimbabwe.
evidence_quote: The ‘designated countries or territories’ are: Andorra, Australia, Barbados, British Virgin Islands, Canada, Cayman Islands, Falkland Islands, Faroe Islands, Gibraltar, Hong Kong, Japan, Monaco, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Republic of Moldova, Republic of North Macedonia, Singapore, South Africa, Switzerland, Taiwan, Ukraine, United Arab Emirates and Zimbabwe.

fact_text: Holders of a licence from a 'designated country or territory' can drive in Great Britain for 12 months and then have up to 5 years from becoming resident to exchange it for a GB licence without taking a test.
evidence_quote: You have 5 years to exchange your licence after becoming resident.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: a foreign licence can be swapped for a GB one at any time. Actually: holders of a 'designated' licence can drive for 12 months and exchange without a test, but only within 5 years of becoming resident. Action required: exchange within 5 years or you must take the GB theory and practical tests.

fact_text: A new resident who holds an EU driving licence and was under 67 when they became resident can keep driving on it until age 70, and may exchange it for a GB licence without retaking the test.
evidence_quote: If you were younger than 67 when you became a resident, you can drive on your EU licence until you’re 70.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: post-Brexit an EU licence must be exchanged immediately. Actually: if you were under 67 when you became resident you can drive on your EU licence until age 70 and can exchange it without retaking your test. Action required: exchange before you turn 70 (or within 3 years if you were 67 or older on becoming resident).
